content: A false alarm, also known as a nuisance alarm, refers to an erroneous report of an emergency situation. This can lead to unnecessary panic and the deployment of emergency resources, such as fire engines, to a location where they are not actually required. Over time, repeated false alarms in a specific area can desensitize individuals to the alarms, causing them to disregard all alarms, assuming they are likely to be false. This phenomenon is reminiscent of Aesop's fable The Boy Who Cried Wolf, where a boy repeatedly raises false alarms about a wolf, leading the townspeople to ignore his cries when a real wolf eventually appears. False alarms can also divert emergency responders from genuine emergencies, potentially resulting in loss of life. In industrial alarm management, a false alarm may refer to an alarm with minimal informational value that can usually be safely disregarded, or to an alarm triggered by a malfunctioning instrument. Both types are problematic due to the cry wolf effect, where repeated false alarms reduce the perceived credibility of future alarms. The term false alarm is somewhat misleading and is often replaced by the term nuisance alarm. When a sensor activates, it is rarely false in the strict sense; rather, it is typically a true reflection of the sensor's current state. The term nuisance more accurately conveys the inconvenience, annoyance, or frustration caused by such alarms. For example, burglar alarms can be triggered by spiders crawling on webs in front of motion detectors, as the motion detector perceives the spider as a large object. A tragic example of the consequences of repeated false alarms occurred at Boland Hall at Seton Hall University on January 19, 2000. Months of false fire alarms led many students to ignore the alarms. When a real fire broke out, three students who disregarded the alarms lost their lives, and many others sustained injuries. Similarly, after numerous false car alarms, people often stop paying attention to determine whether a vehicle is actually being stolen. Even experienced thieves have admitted that car alarms do not deter them, as they assume most alarms will be ignored. In the context of signal detection theory, a false alarm occurs when a non-target event surpasses the detection threshold and is mistakenly identified as a target. This is often referred to in terms of the constant false alarm rate. Additionally, false alarms can describe situations where an individual is startled by something that is later determined to be untrue.
